transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Um, yeah… I guess I’m here because the clinic doctor was kind of on me about how I’ve been eating. I mean, I don’t know, it doesn’t feel that dramatic to me. Most days I just keep it simple—coffee in the morning, and then if I’m between painting jobs I might grab a few bites of something. Sometimes I forget because I’m running around, or I’ve got class paperwork and all these forms pile up, and by the time I get home I’ll have a small dinner if I’m not too busy. So… I guess that’s what they were worried about.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently, or do you consider yourself to be underweight?

I mean… people keep saying that, yeah. My work pants are definitely looser now, like I have to keep pulling them up when I’m on a ladder, which is annoying more than anything. And guys on job sites keep making comments like, “You’re looking really thin,” which… I don’t love people noticing.

But I don’t really think of it as being underweight. I’m on my feet all day, carrying stuff, moving around, climbing up and down, so to me it feels more like I’ve just leaned out from work.
Can you tell me about your eating habits in more detail—do you intentionally limit how much you eat, skip meals, or avoid certain food groups?

Yeah, I mean… I guess I do keep it pretty limited, but it doesn’t feel like a whole “plan” or anything. Most mornings it’s just coffee because I’m trying to get out the door, and then if I’m going between painting jobs I might have a few bites of something, depending on where I am.

It’s hard because sometimes I’m up on ladders or covered in dust or paint, and then I’m thinking about the next place I have to be, and by the time I remember food it’s like… whatever, I’ll just wait. And then at night I’ll have a small dinner if I’m not buried in class paperwork. The forms for that stuff are ridiculous, honestly, they take forever. So yeah… I guess I skip meals, but I don’t think of it like I’m avoiding whole food groups or anything. It’s more that I keep it simple.
Do you worry about gaining weight or becoming fat, even if others might tell you that you're already thin or underweight?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t say I sit there thinking “fat” exactly, that sounds… I don’t know, extreme. But if I eat something really heavy, like pizza or one of those huge sandwiches people bring to a job site, I get this tight, panicky feeling after. Like I’m going to wake up the next morning bigger somehow, or slow, like my body won’t move right.

And with work, you know, I’m climbing ladders and squeezing around rooms with drop cloths everywhere, and if I feel weighed down it’s just… I hate it. It makes me nervous. Like I won’t be able to do what I need to do.
Do you ever make yourself vomit, take laxatives, or exercise excessively to control your weight or shape?

Um… I don’t know. Not really something I’ve thought about like that.

I mean, exercise is sort of a weird word for me because my job is physical already. I’m up and down ladders all day, carrying buckets and rollers and moving furniture around, so when people say “exercise,” I’m like… does work count? Because by the end of the day my arms feel like noodles sometimes.

As far as the other stuff you said, I’m not sure… I mean, no, I don’t have some routine like that. I’ve heard people talk about cleanses and stuff, especially in school—there was this one woman who was always going on about detox teas, and I just remember thinking they sounded disgusting. But yeah, I guess I don’t really do anything like that on purpose.
Do you ever go for long periods without eating, or set strict rules for yourself about what or when you can eat, even if it's not part of a formal diet plan?

Yeah… I mean, I guess that’s kind of why I’m here, because the clinic doctor got on me about it. I don’t really sit down and make rules like “I can’t eat before this time” or whatever, but most days it ends up pretty… small.

Like, coffee in the morning, because I’m usually trying to get my stuff together and get to the job, and then maybe a few bites of something if I’m between places. Sometimes I’ll have a granola bar in the truck, but then I forget it’s there until it’s all melted or crushed, which is gross. And then at night I’ll do a small dinner if I’m not too tired or stuck doing class paperwork. Those forms take forever, I swear.

So… yeah, I can go a long time without eating. I don’t know if I’d call them strict rules, exactly. I just keep it simple.
Do you ever eat a large amount of food in a short period of time, more than most people would eat under similar circumstances, and feel like you can’t stop or control how much you’re eating?

Um… I don’t think so? Like, I know what you mean, kind of, like eating a whole thing of chips without noticing—my cousin does that at barbecues, she’ll stand by the table and just talk and suddenly the bowl is gone, which is kind of funny but also not my thing.

I don’t really have times where I feel like I’m out of control eating a lot. If anything, I get annoyed when food is messy or takes too long, especially if I’ve got paint on me or I’m trying not to get dust all over everything. So… no, I haven’t noticed that happening.
Do you feel like your body looks different than it actually is, or do you worry about specific parts of your body even if others might not notice anything unusual?

I don’t know… I mean, I look in the mirror and it’s just me, you know? I don’t really know what I’m supposed to be seeing versus what’s “actually” there.

Specific parts… not really, I guess. Sometimes work clothes fit weird because they get stiff with paint or drywall dust, and then I’ll be annoyed at how they sit, but that’s more like… I need to wash them or buy better pants, not like some big thing. I had this one pair of overalls that shrank, or I swear they shrank, because they were fine and then suddenly the straps were digging in—anyway, I got rid of them.

So… I’m not sure. I don’t think I see something other people don’t. I just don’t spend a lot of time thinking of it that way.
Do you ever push yourself to do extra physical activity—like climbing more ladders, carrying heavier things, or moving around more—specifically to burn off calories or keep from gaining weight?

I mean… I’m already moving all day for work, so I don’t think I go looking for extra ladders or anything like that on purpose. Ladders are annoying anyway, especially when the feet wobble on old floors—there was this house last month where every room slanted a different way, it was like working on a boat.

But… if I eat something heavy, like pizza or a big sandwich, I do get this kind of panicky feeling after. Like I’ll wake up bigger, or slower, and then I won’t be able to move around the rooms or up and down ladders the way I need to. So I guess I might keep moving more, or feel like I shouldn’t sit too much, but I don’t really think of it as “burning calories” exactly. It’s more like trying not to feel… stuck in my body, I guess.
Do your thoughts about eating, weight, or your body ever interfere with your ability to focus on work, school, or other important parts of your life?

Yeah… I mean, I’m still getting to jobs. I’m not, like, missing whole days because of it or anything. And I’m taking my class still, even though the parking there is ridiculous—there’s this one lot that says “student parking” but it’s always full by, like, 5:30, so you end up circling forever.

But… I have started kind of skipping lunches with people at work. Like if everyone’s going to grab something, I’ll say I have to clean brushes or run to the supply store, which sometimes is true, but not always. And with class, if people want to meet up to study, I usually don’t go if it’s at a café or someone’s bringing food.

It just feels easier if I keep my routine really tight and nobody’s watching or making comments about what I’m doing. So… I guess it does interfere some, socially maybe, but I’m still functioning.
Would you say that how you see yourself or how you feel about yourself is strongly influenced by your weight or the shape of your body?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, if I’m having a bad day, everything feels wrong, but I don’t know if that’s because of my body or just because the job was a mess or someone said something stupid.

Like yesterday, the primer we were using was supposed to dry in an hour and it absolutely did not, and then the whole schedule got messed up, and I was irritated the rest of the day. So if I looked in the mirror then, maybe I’d feel worse about myself, but I don’t know that it’s about shape exactly.

I guess I don’t think, like, “my worth is my weight” or anything like that. That sounds too dramatic. I just… I don’t know. Some days I feel okay, some days I don’t.
Can you think of a time when you tried to eat normally or someone encouraged you to eat more, and how did that make you feel physically and emotionally?

Yeah… there was one time one of the guys on a job was like, “Come on, just eat a real lunch,” and they’d ordered pizza. I tried to just have it and act normal, because everybody was standing around talking about the paint sprayer clogging and whether the trim needed another coat, and I didn’t want to make it a whole thing.

But after I ate it, I felt really uncomfortable. Not even just full—more like panicky, like it was sitting in me and I’d done something I couldn’t undo. I kept thinking I was going to wake up bigger somehow, or heavier, and then the next day I’d be slower going up ladders or moving around tight rooms. Which sounds kind of ridiculous when I say it out loud, because obviously one lunch isn’t going to change how I climb a ladder, but in the moment it feels really real.

Physically I just felt heavy and tense, and emotionally I was kind of… scared, I guess. Like I wanted to keep moving so I didn’t feel trapped in my body.

Have your concerns about eating, weight, or how your body feels affected your ability to participate in social activities, perform at work, or manage other responsibilities, beyond just skipping meals or avoiding certain situations?

I mean… not like I’ve stopped doing everything. I’m still showing up for jobs, and I’m still going to class. Like, if there’s a room that needs cutting in around weird crown molding, I’m there, I’m doing it. Though honestly some of those older houses have walls that aren’t straight at all, and then everyone acts like it’s the paint’s fault.

But yeah, it has affected things some. I don’t really go to lunches with coworkers much anymore, and if people from class want to study somewhere with food or meet at a café, I usually find a reason not to. It just feels easier to keep my routine really tight and not have people noticing or making comments about what I’m doing.

So… I’m functioning, but I guess I’m kind of working around it a lot.
Can you tell me more about how you feel when you think about eating a normal or larger amount of food—does it feel scary, uncomfortable, or something else?

Yeah… scary, I guess. Not in a logical way, because I know a big sandwich isn’t going to, like, instantly change my whole body. But if it’s something heavy—pizza, or a big sandwich, stuff like that—I get this panicky feeling after, like I’m going to wake up bigger somehow.

And then my mind goes to work stuff, which is probably weird. Like, I’ll think, what if I’m slower on ladders, or I can’t move as easily in those little awkward rooms where you’re trying not to bump wet trim or knock into someone’s drop cloth. Some houses are so cramped, too, especially bathrooms where you’re trying to paint behind the toilet and there’s no space to turn around.

So it’s not just “uncomfortable full.” It’s more like… trapped, and worried I won’t be able to move the way I need to.

When you feel scared or panicky after eating something heavy, is it specifically the idea of gaining weight or changing shape that worries you, or is it more about how it affects your ability to work or move?

I think it starts with the weight thing, honestly. Like, if I eat something heavy—pizza, a big sandwich, whatever—I get this panic that I’m going to wake up bigger somehow.

And then it turns into the work stuff in my head, like I’ll be slower on ladders or not able to move around the rooms the way I need to. Especially when you’re in those tight little bathrooms or up against trim and someone’s left tools right where you need to stand—sorry, that’s not really the point.

But yeah… it’s both, I guess. The fear is gaining weight or changing shape, and then my brain connects that to not being able to move right at work.

doctor.question: Would you say that how you see yourself or how you feel about yourself is strongly influenced by your weight or the shape of your body?

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether self-worth or self-evaluation is strongly influenced by weight or body shape, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for overvaluation of weight/shape.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, if I’m having a bad day, everything feels wrong, but I don’t know if that’s because of my body or just because the job was a mess or someone said something stupid.

Like yesterday, the primer we were using was supposed to dry in an hour and it absolutely did not, and then the whole schedule got messed up, and I was irritated the rest of the day. So if I looked in the mirror then, maybe I’d feel worse about myself, but I don’t know that it’s about shape exactly.

I guess I don’t think, like, “my worth is my weight” or anything like that. That sounds too dramatic. I just… I don’t know. Some days I feel okay, some days I don’t.

doctor.question: Can you think of a time when you tried to eat normally or someone encouraged you to eat more, and how did that make you feel physically and emotionally?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I eat something heavy like pizza or a big sandwich, I get this panicky feeling that I'll wake up bigger and slower, and I won't be able to move around ladders and rooms the way I need to.
target_item.reason: The question asks how the patient feels when trying to eat normally or being encouraged to eat more, which most directly relates to the panic and fear of becoming bigger after eating heavier foods.

patient.answer:
Yeah… there was one time one of the guys on a job was like, “Come on, just eat a real lunch,” and they’d ordered pizza. I tried to just have it and act normal, because everybody was standing around talking about the paint sprayer clogging and whether the trim needed another coat, and I didn’t want to make it a whole thing.

But after I ate it, I felt really uncomfortable. Not even just full—more like panicky, like it was sitting in me and I’d done something I couldn’t undo. I kept thinking I was going to wake up bigger somehow, or heavier, and then the next day I’d be slower going up ladders or moving around tight rooms. Which sounds kind of ridiculous when I say it out loud, because obviously one lunch isn’t going to change how I climb a ladder, but in the moment it feels really real.

Physically I just felt heavy and tense, and emotionally I was kind of… scared, I guess. Like I wanted to keep moving so I didn’t feel trapped in my body.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning specifically due to concerns about eating, weight, or shape, which would help differentiate between atypical anorexia (F50.01) and other specified feeding or eating disorder (F50.02).
doctor.question: Have your concerns about eating, weight, or how your body feels affected your ability to participate in social activities, perform at work, or manage other responsibilities, beyond just skipping meals or avoiding certain situations?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for jobs and class, but I’ve started avoiding lunches with coworkers or study meetups because it feels easier to keep my routine tight and not have people commenting on what I’m doing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether eating, weight, or body concerns affect social activities, work performance, or responsibilities, which most directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I mean… not like I’ve stopped doing everything. I’m still showing up for jobs, and I’m still going to class. Like, if there’s a room that needs cutting in around weird crown molding, I’m there, I’m doing it. Though honestly some of those older houses have walls that aren’t straight at all, and then everyone acts like it’s the paint’s fault.

But yeah, it has affected things some. I don’t really go to lunches with coworkers much anymore, and if people from class want to study somewhere with food or meet at a café, I usually find a reason not to. It just feels easier to keep my routine really tight and not have people noticing or making comments about what I’m doing.

So… I’m functioning, but I guess I’m kind of working around it a lot.

doctor.question: Can you tell me more about how you feel when you think about eating a normal or larger amount of food—does it feel scary, uncomfortable, or something else?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I eat something heavy like pizza or a big sandwich, I get this panicky feeling that I'll wake up bigger and slower, and I won't be able to move around ladders and rooms the way I need to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fear or discomfort when considering eating a normal or larger amount, which directly relates to panic about becoming bigger or gaining weight after eating more.

patient.answer:
Yeah… scary, I guess. Not in a logical way, because I know a big sandwich isn’t going to, like, instantly change my whole body. But if it’s something heavy—pizza, or a big sandwich, stuff like that—I get this panicky feeling after, like I’m going to wake up bigger somehow.

And then my mind goes to work stuff, which is probably weird. Like, I’ll think, what if I’m slower on ladders, or I can’t move as easily in those little awkward rooms where you’re trying not to bump wet trim or knock into someone’s drop cloth. Some houses are so cramped, too, especially bathrooms where you’re trying to paint behind the toilet and there’s no space to turn around.

So it’s not just “uncomfortable full.” It’s more like… trapped, and worried I won’t be able to move the way I need to.

doctor.question: When you feel scared or panicky after eating something heavy, is it specifically the idea of gaining weight or changing shape that worries you, or is it more about how it affects your ability to work or move?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I eat something heavy like pizza or a big sandwich, I get this panicky feeling that I'll wake up bigger and slower, and I won't be able to move around ladders and rooms the way I need to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the panic after eating heavy foods is specifically driven by fear of gaining weight or changing shape, which directly matches this symptom.

patient.answer:
I think it starts with the weight thing, honestly. Like, if I eat something heavy—pizza, a big sandwich, whatever—I get this panic that I’m going to wake up bigger somehow.

And then it turns into the work stuff in my head, like I’ll be slower on ladders or not able to move around the rooms the way I need to. Especially when you’re in those tight little bathrooms or up against trim and someone’s left tools right where you need to stand—sorry, that’s not really the point.

But yeah… it’s both, I guess. The fear is gaining weight or changing shape, and then my brain connects that to not being able to move right at work.
